lessons.title: The 2010 Currency War Era: Brazil, the Fed, and QE Spillovers

body.text: In September 2010, Brazil's finance minister Guido Mantega told reporters the world was in the middle of an international currency war. No gold standard was involved, no country announced a devaluation, and yet the accusation stuck, because ultra-loose Fed policy was doing to emerging market currencies exactly what an active devaluation would have done.

children.text: The 1930s currency wars ran through the gold standard: a country left gold, its currency fell, and the mechanism was visible and deliberate. The 2010 currency war ran through interest rates and central bank balance sheets instead, and almost nobody involved called it a devaluation at the time. That is exactly why Mantega's phrase landed so hard. It named a dynamic that developed-market officials were reluctant to admit was happening at all.

markDefs.definition: A central bank buying large quantities of government bonds and other securities to inject money into the financial system, used when interest rates are already near zero and cannot be cut further.

Borrowing in a currency with very low interest rates to invest in assets denominated in a currency with higher interest rates, profiting from the rate gap as long as the exchange rate doesn't move against the trade.

children.text: After the 2008 financial crisis, the US Federal Reserve cut its policy rate to near zero by December 2008 and, once conventional rate cuts were exhausted, turned to
, buying hundreds of billions of dollars of bonds starting in late 2008. With US yields near zero, global investors put on a classic
: borrow cheap dollars, invest in higher-yielding emerging market bonds and equities. The capital had to flow somewhere, and Brazil, India, South Korea and others were the destination.

That capital inflow pushed emerging market currencies up sharply, hurting exactly the exporters those countries were trying to protect. From the receiving end, near-zero US rates and a flood of dollars looked functionally identical to a US devaluation, even though the dollar was simply floating in response to Fed policy rather than being deliberately targeted at a lower level.

body.title: The Road to Mantega's Speech, and What Followed

events.title: Fed rate cut to near zero
events.description: The Fed funds rate is cut to a 0 to 0.25% target range, exhausting conventional rate-cut policy.

events.title: QE1 launched
events.description: The Fed begins large-scale asset purchases to support the financial system and push down long-term yields, the first round of what markets nickname quantitative easing.

events.title: Brazil introduces the IOF tax
events.description: Brazil imposes a 2% tax on foreign portfolio inflows into local fixed income and equities, an early attempt to slow the real's appreciation.

events.title: Mantega's 'currency war' remark
events.description: Brazil's finance minister Guido Mantega tells reporters the world is in the midst of an international currency war, a phrase picked up globally within days.

events.title: Brazil raises the IOF tax further
events.description: Facing continued real appreciation, Brazil raises the tax on foreign fixed income inflows in stages, eventually to 6%, to discourage hot money.

events.title: The Fed announces QE2
events.description: A second round of asset purchases, roughly $600 billion of Treasury securities through mid-2011, intensifying the capital flows emerging markets were already struggling with.

events.title: G20 Seoul Summit
events.description: Leaders agree on non-binding guidelines to monitor current account imbalances and commit, in principle, to move toward market-determined exchange rates and avoid competitive devaluation, without any enforceable mechanism.

body.title: Quick Check: What Made the Fed's Policy Feel Like a Devaluation?
body.question: The Fed never announced a target exchange rate for the dollar during QE1 or QE2. Why did emerging market officials still describe US policy as a form of currency war?
options: Because the Fed explicitly said it wanted a weaker dollar to help US exporters
Because near-zero US rates pushed capital into EM assets, appreciating EM currencies in a way that mirrored the effect of a deliberate US devaluation, even without that intent stated
Because the US formally devalued the dollar against gold, as it had in 1934
Because the IMF ordered the Fed to weaken the dollar as part of the G20 process
body.explanation: The Fed's stated goal was domestic: support the US recovery and fight deflation risk. The effect on EM currencies, sharp appreciation from carry trade inflows, was a side effect rather than a stated target, but the outcome for EM exporters was functionally similar to facing a competitive devaluation. This is why currency war accusations can arise from monetary policy that never explicitly targets the exchange rate at all.

children.text: Brazil Fights Back: Capital Controls Instead of Devaluation

markDefs.definition: Brazil's Imposto sobre Operações Financeiras, a financial transactions tax that Brazil applied to foreign inflows into local fixed income and equity markets to slow currency-appreciating hot money.

children.text: Unlike the 1930s, where the tool was leaving a fixed exchange rate, Brazil's main weapon in 2010 was capital controls. The

taxed foreign money coming in to buy Brazilian bonds, raised in stages through 2010 as the real kept climbing. The logic was straightforward: if you cannot control the Fed's policy and you do not want to devalue outright, tax the inflow itself to blunt its effect on your currency.

children.text: The China Angle: Accused From Both Directions

China occupied an odd position in this fight. The US Congress and Treasury had, for years before 2010, argued that China kept the yuan artificially undervalued through its tight dollar peg, giving Chinese exporters an unfair edge. China had allowed gradual yuan appreciation from 2005 to 2008, then effectively re-pegged to the dollar during the worst of the financial crisis before resuming a slow, managed appreciation from mid-2010, under sustained international pressure. Notably, the US Treasury stopped short of formally labelling China a currency manipulator throughout this period, despite years of Congressional pressure to do so, a step it would only take briefly, and controversially, later in the following decade.

body.text: Notice the shape of the argument. The US accused China of undervaluing the yuan through its peg. Brazil and other emerging markets accused the US of undervaluing the dollar through QE. Almost every major economy in this period considered itself the victim of someone else's currency policy, and almost none considered its own policy the aggressor. That asymmetry, everyone feels wronged, nobody feels responsible, is a recurring feature of currency wars, not a one-off.

columns.label: 1930s
points: Mechanism: leaving a fixed gold parity
Explicit, visible policy action with an announced or obvious new rate
A handful of major economies acting in sequence
Resolved, loosely, by the 1936 Tripartite Agreement
Mechanism: near-zero interest rates and quantitative easing under a floating currency
Indirect, transmitted through capital flows and carry trades rather than an announced rate
One major policy source (the Fed) affecting many emerging markets simultaneously
Addressed only with non-binding G20 guidelines, no enforceable agreement

body.title: Brazilian Real vs US Dollar, 2009 to 2012 (Illustrative)

children.text: Notice the reversal by 2012. Once markets began pricing in an eventual end to ultra-loose Fed policy, the same carry trade flows that had pushed the real up began to unwind, and Brazil's currency gave back much of its gain. Capital that arrives because a rate gap exists tends to leave the moment that gap starts closing, a pattern that returns with force in the 2013 taper tantrum covered later in this course.

body.title: You Sit on an Emerging Market Central Bank's Policy Committee, Late 2010
body.scenario: The Fed has just announced QE2, a further $600 billion in Treasury purchases. Your local currency has appreciated roughly 25% against the dollar over the past 18 months as foreign capital chases the yield gap. Your manufacturing exporters are lobbying hard for relief, but your bond market has benefited from the same inflows, funding government borrowing at unusually low cost.
body.prompt: What tools do you actually have, and what does each one cost you?
body.modelAnswer: You broadly have four options, and none is free. First, a Brazil-style tax on foreign portfolio inflows discourages hot money without touching your policy rate, but it can also deter longer-term foreign direct investment if investors read it as a sign of capital account instability. Second, sterilised intervention, buying dollars in the market and issuing local bonds to soak up the resulting rupee or real liquidity, caps the currency's rise but is expensive to sustain and builds up large forex reserves that carry their own opportunity cost. Third, a South Korea-style macroprudential levy on banks' foreign currency borrowing targets the financial stability risk more precisely than a blanket inflow tax, but takes time to design and negotiate with the banking sector. Fourth, you could simply let the currency appreciate and accept the export pain in exchange for cheaper imports and lower imported inflation, which is the textbook answer but politically the hardest to defend to exporters. Most emerging market policymakers in this period, this committee included, ended up using some combination of the first three rather than picking one cleanly.

body.title: Name the Speech
body.textWithBlank: In September 2010, Brazil's finance minister Guido Mantega said the world was in the midst of an international currency ___, a phrase that came to define this entire episode.
body.explanation: Mantega's 'currency war' remark, made on 27 September 2010, gave this entire QE-driven episode its lasting name, even though the underlying mechanism, interest rates and capital flows under floating exchange rates, was very different from the gold standard exits of the 1930s.

cards.definition: Large-scale central bank purchases of bonds and other securities, used to inject liquidity once policy rates are already near zero.
Borrowing in a low-interest-rate currency to invest in a higher-yielding one, profitable as long as the exchange rate doesn't move against the trade.
Brazil's tax on foreign financial inflows, raised repeatedly in 2009-2010 to slow currency-appreciating hot money.

A formal US Treasury designation for a country judged to be deliberately undervaluing its currency for trade advantage; threatened against China for years but not applied during the 2010 currency war era.
The G20 meeting where leaders agreed non-binding guidelines on current account imbalances and committed, without enforcement, to avoid competitive devaluation.

points: The 2010 currency war ran through near-zero US interest rates and quantitative easing, not through a fixed exchange rate exit like the 1930s.

Cheap dollar funding drove carry trade capital into emerging markets, appreciating their currencies in a way that mirrored the effect of a US devaluation without the Fed ever targeting a lower dollar.
Brazil responded with a rising IOF tax on foreign inflows rather than devaluing its own currency, a fundamentally different tool from anything available in the 1930s.

China was accused of undervaluing the yuan through its dollar peg even as emerging markets accused the US of undervaluing the dollar through QE, showing how currency war blame runs in every direction at once.
The G20's 2010 Seoul guidelines were non-binding, unlike the 1930s' Tripartite Agreement, and did little to stop the underlying dynamic.
Capital that flows in chasing a rate gap tends to reverse once that gap starts closing, setting up the sharp unwind that hit emerging markets, India included, later in the decade.
